title: GLM links and mean maps
dek: A GLM has three moving parts: a linear predictor η = Xβ, a link g(μ) = η, and a variance function V(μ). Mixing them up is how logistic papers report risk ratios by accident.
story: The linear predictor is not the mean. g(μ) = xᵀβ maps a real line η onto the legal range of μ. Identity is fine for a Gaussian mean on ℝ. Logit maps to (0,1). Log maps to (0,∞). Using identity for a probability is a model you can fit in a narrow range and then watch produce μ̂ outside [0,1].

Canonical links make η equal the exponential-family natural parameter. They give nicer IRLS and a globally concave log-likelihood in β for full-rank X in the standard families. They are not morally required: probit and complementary log-log are Bernoulli GLMs with different g.
The inverse link μ = g⁻¹(xᵀβ) is the mean you should plot. Coefficients live on the η scale. exp(β) is a rate ratio for log-linear Poisson and an odds ratio for logit, not a universal “effect size.”
deep: Offset: η = xᵀβ + offset. For incidence, offset = log(person-time). For WGS, sometimes log(coverage). An offset is a coefficient frozen at 1, not a covariate you forgot to estimate.

Non-canonical links lose some exponential-family niceties: IRLS still runs, but the observed Hessian and expected information can disagree more, and the log-likelihood need not be globally concave (rare but real for some links).

Prediction intervals on the μ scale need the inverse link and a variance that includes both Var(β̂) and the GLM’s V(μ). A Normal interval on η, then pushed through g⁻¹, is the usual first move (delta method plate).

Saturated mean: n parameters, μ̂ᵢ = yᵢ (in regular cases). Deviance compares your structured μ(x) to that saturated peak. That is why GLM goodness-of-fit talk is a nested likelihood comparison in disguise.

formulas.label: GLM mean
formulas.expression: g(μᵢ) = xᵢᵀ β   or   μᵢ = g⁻¹(xᵢᵀ β)
formulas.note: β is interpreted on the η = g(μ) scale.

formulas.label: Canonical pairs
formulas.expression: Gaussian: identity;  Bernoulli: logit;  Poisson: log

example.title: Identity versus logit for a probability
example.setup: Linear probability model: μ = β₀ + β_hiv. Logit model: logit μ = β₀ + β_hiv. HIV prevalence in the sample is 0.4, smear-positivity 0.55 overall.

steps.title: Range
steps.body: Identity can predict μ̂ = 1.1 for a high-risk profile. Logit cannot. That is not aesthetic; it is whether μ is a probability.

steps.title: Coefficient units
steps.body: Identity β_hiv is a risk difference. Logit β_hiv is a log odds ratio. Exponentiating an identity coefficient is a mistake.

steps.title: When identity is used anyway
steps.body: For a randomised trial risk difference, identity-binomial or OLS on the binary outcome can be a target-functional choice. Then you own heteroskedasticity and possible μ̂ outside [0,1], and you say so.

example.takeaway: Name g, name the scale of β, name V(μ). Then exp(β) either means something or it does not.

check.prompt: In a log-link Poisson GLM, exp(β_k) is:
choices: A multiplicative shift in the mean μ (a rate ratio if an offset is log exposure)
check.answer: A multiplicative shift in the mean μ (a rate ratio if an offset is log exposure)
check.why: log μ = … + β_k x_k ⇒ μ multiplies by e^{β_k} per unit x. Odds ratios are the logit story.

check.prompt: Logit η = 0. The mean μ = logit⁻¹(0) equals:
On the GLM flow plate, where does the variance function V(μ) live?
choices: In the last arrow, the family that maps μ to the law of Y
In the hat matrix of OLS
check.answer: In the last arrow, the family that maps μ to the law of Y
check.why: Link is the middle arrow. Variance/family is the sampling model of Y given μ.
